summary.text: An internal combustion engine is a heat engine that burns fuel with air in a combustion chamber that is part of the working fluid's flow path.
The hot, high-pressure gas from combustion pushes directly on parts such as pistons, turbine blades, a rotor or a nozzle, turning chemical energy into motion.
German engineer Nicolaus Otto designed the first modern one in 1876, and today most are used in mobile roles such as cars, aircraft and boats.

facts.label: Typical fuels
facts.value: Natural gas, gasoline, diesel fuel or ethanol

facts.label: Main use
facts.value: Mostly mobile: cars, aircraft and boats

facts.label: Diesel's early fuel
facts.value: Rudolf Diesel ran engines on peanut oil by 1900

facts.label: Compression ignition
facts.value: First developed by Rudolf Diesel in 1892

items.prompt: An old boiler heats water, and the steam it makes never touches the flames' exhaust gases before pushing a piston. How does this engine differ from a car engine?

options.label: Its fuel burns far away, so it is not a heat engine
Its working fluid is the burnt fuel gas, like a car's
It burns fuel outside, keeping the working fluid separate
It has no combustion, so no fuel is needed

items.explain: Steam engines are external combustion engines: energy goes to a working fluid not mixed with combustion products, unlike an internal combustion engine.

items.prompt: In one engine design, the expanding burnt gas pushes on a spinning rotor instead of a piston. Which engine is that?

options.label: A Wankel engine
A Stirling engine
A steam piston engine
A two-stroke engine

items.explain: The force can be applied to pistons, turbine blades, a rotor (Wankel engine) or a nozzle.

items.prompt: What energy change takes place when fuel burns in an internal combustion engine and the car moves?

options.label: Motion energy is stored back as fuel
Electrical energy turns into heat
Light from the spark is turned into motion
Chemical energy becomes kinetic energy

items.explain: The process transforms chemical energy into kinetic energy that moves or powers whatever the engine is attached to.

items.prompt: A car's four-stroke engine fires in separate bursts, while a jet or gas turbine burns fuel without stopping. How are these two classes described?

options.label: The car engine is external combustion; the jet is internal
The car has intermittent combustion; the jet has continuous
Both use intermittent combustion, just at different speeds
Neither one counts as an internal combustion engine

items.explain: Piston engines have intermittent combustion, while gas turbines, jet engines and most rocket engines use continuous combustion; all are internal combustion engines.

items.prompt: A farmer wants a renewable fuel for a compression ignition engine, the kind Rudolf Diesel invented. Which fuel fits?

options.label: Bioethanol
Ethyl tert-butyl ether
Biodiesel
Natural gas

items.explain: Biodiesel is a renewable fuel used in compression ignition engines, while bioethanol and ETBE are used in spark ignition engines.

items.prompt: A planner says hydrogen can only come from oil and gas wells. Where can it really come from, for an engine that uses it?

options.label: Only from renewable energy
Only from the air in the combustion chamber
Only from ethanol blended with fossil fuels
Either fossil fuels or renewable energy

items.explain: Hydrogen, though rarely used in these engines, can be obtained from either fossil fuels or renewable energy.
